section.title: Naomi and Ruth Return
section.sectionRationale: This movement completes chapter one: Naomi hears the LORD has visited His people, sets out for home, and releases her daughters-in-law. Orpah turns back, but Ruth clings with a famous vow of covenant loyalty. They arrive in Bethlehem where Naomi pours out her bitterness. It is one unit built on the repeated word return and the contrast between turning back and cleaving.
section.thesis: As Naomi turns home empty and bitter, a Moabite widow binds herself to Naomi's people and Naomi's God in astonishing covenant loyalty, so that the barley harvest and Ruth's presence become the first quiet signs that God has not abandoned the emptied.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the road home and the plea to turn back; Orpah's departure and Ruth's vow; the arrival in Bethlehem; and Naomi's lament, Call me Mara.

units.label: The road home and the plea to turn back
units.note: the LORD has visited His people

verses.text: When Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food, she and her daughters-in-law prepared to leave the land of Moab.
Accompanied by her two daughters-in-law, she left the place where she had been living and set out on the road leading back to the land of Judah.
Then Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home. May the LORD show you {{chesed|loving devotion}}, as you have shown to your dead and to me.
May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” And she kissed them as they wept aloud
and said, “Surely we will {{shuv|return}} with you to your people.”

units.label: Orpah turns back, Ruth clings
units.note: your people will be my people

verses.text: But Naomi replied, “Return home, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Are there still sons in my womb to become your husbands?
Return home, my daughters. Go on, for I am too old to have another husband. Even if I thought there was hope for me to have a husband tonight and to bear sons,
would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from having husbands? No, my daughters, it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.”
Again they wept aloud, and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth {{dabaq|clung}} to her.
“Look,” said Naomi, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.”

But Ruth replied: “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.”
When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.

units.label: Arrival in Bethlehem and Naomi's lament

verses.text: So Naomi and Ruth traveled until they came to Bethlehem. When they entered Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?”
“Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me {{mara|Mara}}, because the {{shaddai|Almighty}} has dealt quite bitterly with me.
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? After all, the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has afflicted me.”
So Naomi returned from the land of Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess. And they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant love, loyal kindness that goes beyond mere duty. It is the great theme of Ruth, shown by Ruth to Naomi, by Boaz to both women, and supremely by the LORD to them all. The BSB footnote at verse 8 notes its wide range: love, goodness, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and loyalty to a covenant.

shuv.gloss: To return, turn back, or turn around. The verb sounds through chapter one again and again as Naomi returns to Bethlehem and urges her daughters-in-law to turn back to Moab. Ruth's refusal to turn back is the hinge of the chapter; the same root elsewhere in Scripture carries the sense of turning to God in repentance and faith.

dabaq.gloss: To cling, cleave, hold fast, stick to. It is the very word used in Genesis 2:24 of a husband cleaving to his wife. Here Ruth cleaves to Naomi with a loyalty as strong as a marriage bond: Orpah kisses and leaves, but Ruth clings and will not let go.

mara.gloss: Bitter. Naomi renames herself Mara, bitter, in place of Naomi, pleasant, confessing that the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her. Her lament is honest and raw, yet the reader already sees the barley harvest and faithful Ruth as signs that her emptiness is not the end of the story.

shaddai.gloss: The Almighty, an ancient title for God stressing His overwhelming power and all-sufficiency. Naomi twice names God as Shaddai, the One she believes has afflicted her. The same title fills the book of Job, another believer wrestling honestly with God's hidden hand in suffering; and the Almighty who empties Naomi is the very One quietly working her rescue.

basic.context: Naomi hears that the famine in Judah has lifted and decides to go home. On the road she urges both widowed daughters-in-law to turn back to Moab and find new husbands. Orpah tearfully goes back, but Ruth refuses, binding herself to Naomi with a beautiful vow: your people will be my people, your God my God. They reach Bethlehem, where Naomi tells the women to call her Mara, bitter, because she left full and has come back empty.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative that turns on a single repeated word, return or turn back, and on the contrast between Orpah who turns back and Ruth who clings. Ruth's vow is one of the great confessions of loyalty in the Bible. Naomi's bitter complaint is honest lament, not unbelief to be scolded; she rightly sees God's hand, even if she cannot yet see His kindness.
basic.originalLanguages: The word shuv, to return or turn back, drums through the chapter as Naomi returns and presses the others to go back. Ruth instead dabaq, clings, the same word for a husband cleaving to his wife. Naomi asks to be called Mara, bitter, and names God as Shaddai, the Almighty, who she feels has emptied her. And she prays chesed, loving devotion, over the very daughters she is sending away.
basic.typology: Ruth the Moabite outsider, joining herself by faith to the LORD and His people, is a living picture of the nations being grafted in, fulfilled when the gospel goes to the Gentiles. Her covenant vow foreshadows the deeper cleaving of the redeemed to God, and the barley harvest hints at the provision God is about to pour out.
basic.christ: Ruth, an outsider brought near, stands in the line that leads to Christ, and her welcome into God's people previews the day when people from every nation would be included through Jesus. Naomi's move from empty to full, still only hinted here, traces the gospel shape of loss reversed by a redeemer, which Christ accomplishes in full.
basic.god: God is at work behind the scenes: He has visited His people with bread, He is drawing Ruth to Himself, and He is steering Naomi home just as the harvest begins. Naomi feels only His heavy hand, yet the reader sees His faithful loving devotion quietly surrounding her even in her bitterness.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 23 marked Moabites as outsiders, which makes Ruth's inclusion striking. Matthew 1 names Ruth in Jesus' family tree. And Ephesians 2 describes how those once far off are brought near, the very thing happening to Ruth.
basic.oneStory: The one great story of God gathering a people to Himself moves forward as a Moabite widow says, your God will be my God. Naomi comes home empty and bitter, but Ruth's loyalty and the opening harvest are the first signs that God is about to fill the empty, foreshadowing the Redeemer who welcomes outsiders and turns mourning into joy.

context.literary: The chapter's second half is built on a single Hebrew leitmotif, the verb shuv, return or turn back, which recurs so often across verses 6 through 22 that its repetition becomes the passage's real structuring device more than any change of scene. Naomi presses the command in triplicate, return, verse 8, return, verse 11, return once more, verse 12, an intensifying refrain that makes Ruth's eventual refusal land as a genuine act of resistance against mounting pressure rather than a single easy yes. Ruth's own vow, verses 16 and 17, answers that triple refrain with a matching structure of its own, four parallel clauses, where you go, where you live, your people, your God, followed by a fifth that raises the stakes to death and burial, and then a self-maledictory oath, may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, the very covenant curse formula Israel's own narrators use elsewhere for the gravest promises, 1 Samuel 14:44, 2 Samuel 3:9. The scene then resolves with unusual speed, Naomi stops trying to persuade her, verse 18, a narrative shorthand for a decision that in life would have taken far longer to reach. The arrival at Bethlehem is staged as public spectacle, the whole town stirred, before narrowing to Naomi's private lament, and the unit closes on a single, quiet notice of timing, the beginning of the barley harvest, planting a seed the next chapter will immediately water.
context.historical: A widow without husband or living sons occupied one of the most precarious positions in the ancient world, with no independent right to inherit her husband's land and no guaranteed provider once her sons were gone, which is exactly what makes Naomi's blessing in verse 9, that the LORD grant each daughter-in-law rest in a new husband's home, so pointed; that rest meant security and provision, not mere relaxation, the very word Naomi will use again of Ruth's future in 3:1. Naomi's rhetorical questions in verses 11 to 13, are there still sons in my womb, assume the ancient custom later codified as levirate marriage, in which a brother-in-law married a childless widow to raise up an heir in the dead man's name, Deuteronomy 25:5-10; Naomi's point is not merely that she is too old to remarry but that even a hypothetical new son could not be born and raised in time to help two young widows now. Moab itself, worshiping Chemosh, made Ruth's declared allegiance to the LORD in verse 16 a genuine renunciation of her own people's god, not a minor courtesy. Bethlehem's excitement at Naomi's return, the whole town was stirred, fits a small agricultural settlement where a widow's homecoming after roughly a decade's absence, accompanied by a foreign daughter-in-law, would have been immediate public news, and the note that they arrived at the start of the barley harvest anchors the scene in springtime, when the poor and the gleaners would soon have their one seasonal opportunity to gather food from the standing grain.
context.canonical: Ruth's declaration, your people will be my people, your God will be my God, joins a line of outsiders who cross into covenant with the LORD by confession rather than by birth, a pattern that includes Rahab's confession that the LORD is God in heaven above and on earth below, Joshua 2:11, and that Israel's own law anticipated by making room for the sojourner who wished to keep the Passover, Exodus 12:48. Naomi's demand that her daughters-in-law return to their mother's house, verse 8, rather than the more usual father's house, is itself unusual enough that some read it as a mark of the narrator's care for small domestic realism, a household of women speaking to women about women's futures. The self-maledictory oath Ruth swears, may the LORD punish me, uses the same formula that later marks the gravest promises in Israel's court and army, 1 Samuel 14:44 and 2 Samuel 3:9, showing that a Moabite woman has, within a single speech, adopted not only Israel's God but Israel's very idiom for binding speech. The chapter's last word, the beginning of the barley harvest, is a canonical hinge as deliberate as any in Scripture, since the next chapter opens directly inside that harvest, and the whole remaining plot, gleaning, redemption, marriage, and the birth that closes the book, unfolds within the few weeks that single clause has just opened.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The author stages three responses to hardship side by side so that readers must weigh them rather than simply admire the obvious hero. Naomi's counsel to return is not selfish; it is generous, urging two young women toward the only realistic security their culture offered, a new marriage among their own people. Orpah's choice to accept that counsel is never criticized in the text; she does exactly what she is told to do. Ruth alone goes further than instructed, and the narrator wants that excess noticed, a loyalty that outruns even the reasonable release Naomi offers her. At the same time the author refuses to let Naomi's bitterness be softened or explained away; her raw complaint in verses 20 and 21 is allowed to stand as the chapter's near final word, so that the reader learns two things at once, that costly loyalty is possible even from an outsider with every reason to leave, and that honest grief before God is not disqualifying faith but a form of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Naomi's counsel to Orpah and Ruth describes wise, culturally realistic advice under the conditions of her time; it is not a command that widows in every era must remarry within their own community, nor is Orpah's choice to follow that advice ever treated as a failure to be corrected. Ruth's vow, similarly, is not held up as a rule that every convert must abandon every tie to family, only as one particular, costly example of covenant loyalty that the book commends by its outcome rather than by direct command. Naomi's lament is likewise descriptive of grief, not prescriptive of despair; the text lets her call herself Mara without either endorsing the accusation that God has wronged her or rebuking her for saying so. What remains binding for readers in every era is the character these events display rather than the specific choices themselves, steadfast love that costs something real, and lament that still addresses God rather than abandoning Him.

debates.question: Is Naomi's lament in verses 20 and 21 a failure of faith or faithful honesty before God?

views.label: Faithful lament
views.case: Naomi speaks truly: God is sovereign over her suffering, and she brings her bitterness straight to Him rather than denying it, in the pattern of the Psalms and Job. This is faith wrestling, not faith abandoned.

views.label: Faith clouded by grief
views.case: She calls herself empty while Ruth, who will prove better than seven sons, stands beside her, and she cannot yet see the kindness of God at work; her words show real but limited sight, a faith dimmed by pain.

debates.bearing: Both readings honor the text: God welcomes honest lament, and He is also kindly at work beyond what the sufferer can presently see, so grief and hope can be held together.

debates.question: Why does the narrator highlight that Ruth is a Moabitess?

views.label: To magnify grace to the outsider
views.case: Moab was an enemy nation under a curse of exclusion, so naming Ruth a Moabitess again and again underscores the wonder that she is brought into God's people and into the Messiah's line by faith.

views.label: To set up the theme of inclusion
views.case: The repeated label prepares the reader for the surprise of chapter four, where a Moabite widow becomes the great-grandmother of King David, showing God's purpose to gather the nations.

debates.bearing: Either way, Ruth's Moabite identity is not incidental; it displays the reach of God's covenant mercy beyond Israel, a foretaste of the gospel to all peoples.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens on a report that the LORD had paqad, attended to, His people by giving them bread, verse 6, the same verb used when the LORD attended to Sarah as He had promised and she conceived Isaac, Genesis 21:1, and when He attended to the Israelites in their Egyptian slavery and their prayers reached Him, Exodus 4:31. The word names a purposeful, gracious intervention, not a passing glance, and its use here quietly signals, before Naomi ever complains, that God's action toward His people has already begun; the news that reaches Naomi in Moab is itself the first fruit of that visitation, and everything that follows in the book, the return, Ruth's vow, the harvest, the redemption, unfolds inside a story God had already started before anyone in the story could ask Him to.

Naomi's blessing in verse 9, that each woman find menuchah, rest, uses a term meaning far more than repose; it names the settled security of a home, a husband's provision, land under a family's control, the very rest Israel was promised in the land itself, Deuteronomy 12:9. The word returns with pointed force in 3:1, when Naomi asks whether she should not seek menuchah for Ruth, so that the blessing spoken here in resignation becomes, two chapters later, a plan Naomi actively pursues.

Ruth's oath in verse 17, may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, is not free composition but a fixed idiom that Israel's own narrators use for the gravest, most binding promises, spoken by Saul over Jonathan and by Abner in the wars of David, 1 Samuel 14:44, 2 Samuel 3:9. A Moabite woman speaks Israel's own covenant courtroom language as fluently as any native son, a detail easy to miss in translation but startling in the original.

Orpah's very name may echo oreph, the back of the neck, a small but likely deliberate wordplay for the sister-in-law who, understandably and without rebuke from the text, turns her back and returns to her mother's house; Ruth, by contrast, is never given a name that explains her loyalty, as though the narrator wants her faithfulness to be a free act rather than a fate written into her name from birth.

Naomi's lament plays two more words against each other. She went away full and returns empty, reqam, the same word Scripture uses elsewhere for a servant sent away with nothing, Genesis 31:42, or an offering that must never be brought empty-handed, Exodus 23:15. The contrast is total, not partial, in the Hebrew's own accounting, and Naomi feels every bit of that totality even though the reader already knows, from the very next clause, that she has returned at the beginning of the barley harvest, an empty word about to be answered by a full field.

typology.type: Ruth the Moabitess joined by faith to the LORD and His people
typology.fulfillment: Ruth renounces her own people and her own gods in a single breath, your people will be my people, your God will be my God, becoming, within the story, the clearest Old Testament picture of a Gentile grafted into Israel by confession rather than birth. Paul later describes exactly this grafting in olive tree terms, a wild branch joined to the root that once excluded it, Romans 11:17-18, and insists that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, Galatians 3:28. Ruth's vow falls short only in scale, one woman's private decision rather than a whole world's reconciliation, which is precisely the wider work the gospel goes on to accomplish.

typology.type: Ruth's covenant vow, your God will be my God
typology.fulfillment: The new covenant promise, I will be their God and they will be My people, Jeremiah 31:33, is exactly the bond Ruth speaks into being for herself centuries early, uninvited and unrequired, simply because she has come to love the God she has only recently met through Naomi's household. The vow costs her everything familiar, homeland, family gods, likely a second marriage among her own people, and asks nothing in return but Naomi's continued presence. It anticipates the free, costly cleaving of every believer who comes to say the same words to the LORD without any promise of ease attached.

typology.type: Naomi returning empty at the start of harvest
typology.fulfillment: Naomi arrives with nothing, no husband, no sons, no plan, at the exact moment the barley harvest is beginning, a timing too precise to be incidental in a book this carefully constructed. The pattern, emptiness met immediately by provision already underway, anticipates the fuller reversal Christ works, turning the mourning of His people into joy, John 16:20, and supplying, out of apparent nothing, more than enough, as at the feeding of the five thousand, John 6:1-13. Naomi cannot yet see the harvest as anything but background detail; the reader is meant to see it as the first sentence of her answered prayer.

study.christ:
Ruth's vow, wherever you go I will go, is a costly promise to follow; the gospel's better news runs the direction the other way. Jesus tells His disciples that He goes to prepare a place for them and will come again to receive them to Himself, so that where He is, there they may be also, John 14:2-3. Ruth binds herself to accompany Naomi into an uncertain future; Christ binds Himself to bring His people into a certain one, His own presence, and does the harder half of the journey Himself, coming down before He calls anyone to follow.

Naomi's blessing over her daughters-in-law, that the LORD grant each of them rest in a new home, voices exactly the longing Jesus later answers directly, come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest, Matthew 11:28. What Naomi can only pray for as a distant hope, security under a husband's roof, Christ offers as an immediate gift to anyone who comes to Him, no marriage, lineage, or nationality required.

Ruth's self-maledictory oath, may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, invokes curse upon herself to guarantee a promise; the writer of Hebrews describes God doing something greater still, swearing by Himself since there is nothing higher to swear by, so that His promise to Abraham's heirs, and through them to all who take refuge in Christ, would be utterly certain, Hebrews 6:13-18. Ruth's oath is a creature binding herself to a fellow creature; God's oath is the Creator binding Himself to His own promise, and it is that oath, not Ruth's, that finally secures the line running to Jesus.

And Naomi's bitter question, why call me Naomi, when the LORD has emptied me, finds its answer not in this chapter but in the empty tomb that stands behind every gospel promise of reversal, a God who specializes in bringing the full out of the empty, life out of death, and, in Naomi's own small story, a grandson out of a house that had buried every man in it.
study.god:
This is the first passage in the book where anyone names God directly and repeatedly, and it is striking that the one doing the naming is a grieving woman leveling an accusation. Naomi credits the LORD with attending to His people, verse 6, then twice attributes her own suffering to Him by name, the hand of the LORD has gone out against me, verse 13, and the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me, verse 20, going so far as to say the LORD has testified against me, verse 21, courtroom language, as though she stood accused and God were the witness for the prosecution. The narrator never corrects her theology. Naomi is not wrong that the LORD is sovereign over her losses; she is simply not yet able to see, from where she stands, the good He is already working through them.

This matters for how Scripture teaches its readers to speak to God in suffering. Naomi's raw, accusing prayer stands beside Job's similarly blunt confession, the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away, Job 1:21, as evidence that lament, even lament that names God as the source of one's pain, belongs inside faith rather than outside it. What is not permitted in Scripture is silence that pretends God is irrelevant to suffering; what is welcomed, again and again, is speech that brings the suffering directly to Him.

The chapter also shows God working through entirely ordinary channels, a rumor of good harvests reaching a foreign country, a widow's decision to walk home, a foreign daughter-in-law's stubborn loyalty, none of it miraculous in the way a burning bush or a parted sea is miraculous. This is a God who is just as active in timing a harvest and steering a decision as He is in any grander display of power, and readers are meant to notice that His providence over Naomi's return is no less real, no less His own doing, for having no thunder attached to it. The God who seems, by Naomi's own account, to have emptied her is the same God already filling her hands again, one barley stalk and one loyal daughter-in-law at a time, before she has any way of knowing it.

crossReferences.note: Moabites were barred from entering the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation, a penalty for their nation's history of hostility toward Israel in the wilderness. Ruth's welcome into Israel by personal confession rather than genealogy, and her place in David's own line, is a striking exception that the rest of Scripture treats as grace overriding a standing legal barrier.

The women of Bethlehem later tell Naomi that Ruth, who loves her, is better to her than seven sons. The chapter's own claim that Naomi returned empty is answered, by the book's end, with a daughter-in-law whose love outweighs the very loss Naomi is mourning here.

Paul describes Gentiles as once separate from Christ, excluded from citizenship in Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, now brought near by the blood of Christ. Ruth's declaration, your people will be my people, your God will be my God, is exactly this nearness, centuries early, offered to a Moabite by grace rather than law.

Ruth is named plainly in the genealogy that opens the New Testament, a Moabitess placed without embarrassment inside the Messiah's own family tree. The vow she swears in this chapter is the very loyalty that puts her there.

The LORD attended to Sarah as He had promised, and she conceived Isaac in her old age. The same verb describes the LORD attending to His people with bread in Ruth 1:6, tying the news that draws Naomi home to the same kind of purposeful, life-giving visitation that once opened Sarah's womb.

The law of levirate marriage required a brother-in-law to marry a childless widow and raise up an heir in his dead brother's name. Naomi's question, are there still sons in my womb to become your husbands, only makes sense against this custom, and it sets up the very redeemer role Boaz will later fill.

Saul swears, may God punish me, and ever so severely, if Jonathan must not die for breaking the fast, the same fixed formula Ruth uses to bind herself to Naomi. A Moabite widow's vow is framed in the identical courtroom language Israel's own king uses for his gravest oaths.

Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to Him and find rest. Naomi can only pray that her daughters-in-law might find such rest in a human marriage; the gospel offers the same gift, rest, immediately from Christ Himself, open to any who come.

Job blesses the name of the LORD even as he confesses that the LORD has taken away what He gave. Naomi's harder words, the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me, stand in the same tradition of honest lament that still addresses God directly rather than walking away from Him.

God promises Abram that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. Ruth the Moabite, binding herself to Abram's God and Abram's people in this very chapter, is one of Scripture's clearest pictures of that ancient promise beginning to reach beyond Israel's own borders.

study.oneStory:
When the LORD called Abram, He promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, a promise that from the beginning pointed outward, toward peoples who were not yet Abram's own. Ruth's vow in this chapter, your people will be my people, your God will be my God, is that ancient promise beginning to run in reverse, not Abram's family reaching out to bless a Moabite, but a Moabite reaching in to claim the blessing for herself, unasked and unearned, on nothing but her own confession of loyalty and faith.

This is redemption's pattern in miniature: an outsider, from a nation under long-standing covenant suspicion, Deuteronomy 23:3-6, crosses every visible boundary, nationality, religion, family loyalty, to bind herself to the LORD's people, and the text does not treat this as scandalous but as exactly the kind of loyalty the book wants its readers to admire. Centuries of redemptive history are compressed into one woman's few verses of speech.

Naomi's own arc, full to empty, sits inside the same larger story. She returns to Bethlehem with nothing recognizable as blessing, no husband, no sons, only a foreign daughter-in-law and bitter words for God, yet the chapter's very last clause, they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest, quietly insists that emptiness and provision can occupy the same sentence, the same moment, without either canceling the other. This is the shape the whole Bible will keep tracing, loss that looks final giving way to a harvest that has, in fact, already begun.

The line runs forward from here through Boaz, Obed, Jesse, and David, and further still to the day when a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue will stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9, the promise to Abram finally answered without remainder. A Moabite widow's stubborn love for her mother-in-law's God turns out to be one of the small, unlikely hinges on which that whole enormous story swings.

sermon.title: God of the Ordinary
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Ruth, this message treats Ruth 1:19-22, the return to Bethlehem and Naomi's lament, Call me Mara, showing God's providence at work in ordinary loss and homecoming. A faithful, expository handling of the close of this movement.

quiz.q: What did Ruth vow to Naomi on the road to Judah?

options.text: Where you go I will go; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
options.note: Ruth 1:16-17 records her famous vow of covenant loyalty and faith.

options.text: That she would find Naomi a new husband in Bethlehem.
options.note: Ruth pledged herself to Naomi, not to arranging a marriage for her.

options.text: That she would return to Moab if life in Judah proved hard.
options.note: She vowed the opposite: only death would separate them.

options.text: That she would keep worshiping the gods of Moab.
options.note: She renounced Moab's gods and embraced the LORD as her God.

quiz.q: How did Orpah and Ruth respond differently to Naomi's plea?

options.text: Orpah turned back to Moab, but Ruth clung to Naomi and would not leave.
options.note: Ruth 1:14 contrasts Orpah's kiss goodbye with Ruth clinging to Naomi.

options.text: Both turned back, but Ruth returned later.
options.note: Ruth never turned back; she clung from the start, unlike Orpah.

options.text: Both refused and went with Naomi.
options.note: Only Ruth went on; Orpah returned to her people.

options.text: Orpah went with Naomi and Ruth stayed in Moab.
options.note: It was the reverse: Ruth went and Orpah stayed.

quiz.q: Why did Naomi ask to be called Mara?

options.text: Mara means bitter, and she felt the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her, emptying her of husband and sons.
options.note: Ruth 1:20-21 records her lament that she went out full and came back empty.

options.text: Mara was the name of her homeland in Moab.
options.note: Mara is not a place name; it means bitter and expresses her grief.

options.text: She wanted to honor a relative named Mara.
options.note: The name is chosen for its meaning, bitter, not for a relative.

options.text: She had converted to a new religion.
options.note: The name change reflects grief, not a change of faith.

quiz.q: What detail at the end of chapter one hints at hope to come?

options.text: They arrive in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
options.note: Ruth 1:22 signals God's provision beginning, setting up the gleaning of chapter two.

options.text: Naomi is immediately given a new husband.
options.note: No new husband is given; the hopeful sign is the harvest and Ruth's presence.

options.text: The famine returns to Moab.
options.note: The hopeful note is provision in Judah, not disaster in Moab.

options.text: Orpah changes her mind and follows them.
options.note: Orpah does not return; the hope lies in the harvest and in Ruth.

quiz.q: What is striking about Ruth being repeatedly called a Moabitess?

options.text: Moab was an enemy nation, so her welcome into God's people shows the wide reach of His grace.
options.note: Her inclusion previews the gathering of the nations, fulfilled in the gospel.

options.text: It shows she never truly belonged and was only tolerated.
options.note: She is fully welcomed and even placed in the Messiah's line, not merely tolerated.

options.text: It proves the book is only about Moab, not Israel.
options.note: The book is set in Israel and points to David; her Moabite origin magnifies grace.

options.text: It is an unimportant detail with no meaning.
options.note: The repeated label is deliberate, highlighting grace to an outsider.

questions: Ruth gave up her homeland, her people, and her old gods to follow the LORD. What has following God cost you, and what has it been worth?
Orpah made a reasonable, safe choice to go back; Ruth made a costly choice to cling. Where is God calling you to costly loyalty rather than the safe road back?
Naomi brought her bitterness honestly to God rather than pretending. How does her example free you to lament truthfully while still trusting Him?
Ruth, an outsider, was welcomed into God's people by faith. How does this shape the way you welcome those who feel far off from God?
God had quietly provided bread and was drawing Ruth in, even while Naomi felt empty. Where might God be at work in your life in ways you have not yet noticed?

translationNotes.note: Loving devotion renders the Hebrew chesed, covenant loyalty and steadfast love; the BSB footnote notes its range of love, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and covenant loyalty.
Clung renders dabaq, the same verb used in Genesis 2:24 of a husband cleaving to his wife, marking Ruth's loyalty as covenant-strong.
Naomi means pleasant and Mara means bitter; the wordplay turns her own name into a lament. Almighty renders Shaddai, also in verse 21.
I went away full but the LORD has brought me back empty frames the book's central reversal, from emptiness to the fullness God will provide.
